newsitem.title: USA: Lawmakers no longer see US heat oil supply crunch.
newsitem.headline: Lawmakers no longer see US heat oil supply crunch.

text.p: New England lawmakers who last month raised alarm over low heating oil stocks said Monday they no longer saw a supply crunch ahead for this winter but remained concerned about high prices.
"It appears now that it is very unlikely there will be a crisis of supply," said Sen. Joseph Lieberman, a Connecticut Democrat.

Speaking to reporters after a meeting with Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary, Lieberman said with heating oil prices up 20 to 25 cents a gallon from a year ago, refiners had bolstered output of heating oil to meet demand.
"But it does mean that our consumers and businesses are going to pay 20 to 25 cents more today for home heating oil," Lieberman told reporters.

Lieberman and Democrats Sen. Christopher Dodd of Connecticut and Rep. Joseph Kennedy of Massachusetts met with O'Leary Monday to discuss the outcome of her meetings October 18 and 25 with oil industry officials and futures market regulators in response to the lawmakers' concerns.
"Basically the three of us said that this is not a situation that we find acceptable," Lieberman said.
Energy Department officials have repeatedly said that they have no plans to step into the heating oil futures or physical markets to cap prices or beef up stocks.
Before Monday's meeting, Kennedy said he was looking for O'Leary to outline more "proactive steps" to counteract refiners' efforts to keep their inventories lean.

No new proposals came out of the meeting, but Kennedy said that the Congressmen had promised within the next seven to 10 days to supply a list of actions that could be put in place to deal with the short-term problem and the longer-term problem of chronically low inventories.

Dodd, who is chairman of the Democratic party, said the Clinton administration had helped to ease the price hit for the elderly and the poor by releasing federal funds for low-income heating assistance early.
But Kennedy added that the higher prices were "tantamount to a 20 percent reduction in LIHEAP (low-income home energy assistance program) funding for this winter."

The lawmakers said they would be willing to support any legislation the Energy Department needed to be able to release oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve if necessary to bolster oil supplies or set up a regional heating oil reserve.
O'Leary said 10 days ago that the Energy Department would complete a study by April on the feasibility of setting up a product reserve, but noted that past studies had shown it would be impractical.
